**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

The world you entered was in the middle of national mourning.

Fourteen days before your birth, King George VI died at Sandringham at 56 — younger than most expected, his health worn down by years of smoking and the strain of the war. His daughter Elizabeth was in Kenya when she was told; she flew home as Queen. The coronation was still fifteen months away. Britain was adjusting, in that quiet and formal way it adjusts to things, to the fact that the Elizabethan age had begun. You were born into its opening weeks — a reign that would last until 2022, outlasting most of what seemed permanent in 1952.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the Oslo Winter Olympics were at their midpoint — the Games ran February 14 to 25, and February 20 fell squarely in competition. Norway dominated on home snow, particularly in the cross-country events, in front of crowds that experienced the Games almost entirely through radio and newspaper. Television was not yet the medium through which the world watched sport. That transformation was still a few years away.

---

**The Korean War** had become something stranger than a war. The front lines had barely moved in a year. Fighting continued — men were dying — but what was stalled wasn't the military situation so much as a single negotiating question: what to do with prisoners of war. The United Nations insisted on voluntary repatriation; any POW who did not wish to return home should not be forced to go. China and North Korea demanded the return of all prisoners, regardless of their wishes. Armistice talks at Panmunjom had been running since July 1951 and had ground to a halt over this one point of principle. The deadlock would last another sixteen months and cost tens of thousands more lives. You were born into a war that was simultaneously frozen and ongoing, with no resolution in sight.

---

**The jet age had not yet arrived.** The de Havilland Comet — the world's first commercial jet airliner — would make its first passenger flight on May 2, 1952, ten weeks after your birth. The world you entered was still traveled by propeller. The crossing from New York to London took the better part of a day by air, longer by ship. What seemed like ordinary speed in February 1952 would feel archaic within a decade.

Harry Truman was in the White House, and in these weeks Dwight Eisenhower had just made clear he would seek the Republican nomination. The contest against Robert Taft was building. The America you'd grow up in — shaped by Eisenhower's caution and Cold War consensus — hadn't quite started yet.

---

**Ten years later, same date**: On February 20, 1962, John Glenn climbed into *Friendship 7* and became the first American to orbit the Earth. Three orbits. Four hours and fifty-five minutes. You turned ten that morning and the country stopped around you. Schools brought televisions into classrooms. It was your birthday, and it was the day the space race visibly shifted.

---

**Seventy-four years.**

You were born into a world where the hydrogen bomb had not yet been tested — that came in November 1952, nine months after your birth, multiplying the destructive scale of nuclear weapons by a factor of hundreds. The Soviet empire was at its maximum extent, Stalin alive and still in power. The colonial map of Africa was largely intact. The first computer program had been run just three years before your birth and computers were still machines that filled rooms, operated by specialists, touching no part of ordinary life.

The Queen who came to the throne a fortnight before you were born reigned for seventy years and died in 2022. You were there for almost all of it — the coronation, the jubilees, the whole long arc of the postwar world she presided over. The world that mourned her father in February 1952 and the world that mourned her in September 2022 were separated by everything: technology, politics, medicine, the shape of the map, the texture of daily life.

You've moved through all of it, from one side to the other.
